narrative.text: Concurrent conditions and parallel processes. “A focal sensory neuropathy of the right superficial peroneal nerve is described”. Right superficial peroneal nerve involvement can produce local sensory leg manifestations and coexist with radiculopathy. It does not explain all four limbs or the autonomic complaints. Nerve conduction and the EMG summary describe a right-sided focal sensory axonal lesion. Ultrasound gives additional structural information but does not determine its cause. Left-sided and radicular changes are assessed separately. “Multilevel degenerative spinal changes with described chronic radiculopathies”. Chronic L5 and S1 radiculopathies and degenerative changes may separately explain part of the local sensory and pain manifestations. They are not equated with the cause of the whole widespread syndrome. ENMG describes chronic inactive L5–S1 radiculopathies bilaterally; there are structural lumbar and historical cervical/thoracic changes. They explain part of the manifestations, but their correspondence to all widespread sensory and autonomic complaints is not proven.

emphasis_terms: Incidental change of the endometrium/uterine junctional zone on MRI
narrative.text: Incidental findings. “Incidental change of the endometrium/uterine junctional zone on MRI”. The endometrial change was incidentally described on spinal MRI; its link to the neurological manifestations or bone lesions is not proven. A separate gynecological assessment is needed. Heterogeneity of the endometrial signal and junctional zone contour is described; there is no specialized gynecological assessment. Neoplasia is not established, and clinical significance depends on symptoms and targeted study.

emphasis_terms: Document discrepancies and limited representativeness of individual results
narrative.text: Data quality and representativeness. “Document discrepancies and limited representativeness of individual results”. Unit discrepancies, unestablished dates, incomplete protocols and different types of bone marrow material affect data interpretation. This is a question of their quality and completeness, not a separate diagnosis. There are contradictory units in the light chain retelling, undated tests, unknown drugs and an incomplete neurophysiological protocol. A hypocellular aspirate and an adequate normocellular trephine specimen are different materials; they should not be considered automatically mutually exclusive.
Source support of the synthesis: 21. For each source the accepted statement and its applicability to the clinical question are given.

“American Society of Hematology 2026 guidelines on diagnosis of light chain amyloidosis”. Bone marrow Congo red testing can give false-negative and false-positive results; a positive result alone is not sufficient grounds for amyloid-directed treatment. Proper amyloid typing requires suitable tissue and an appropriate method, including mass spectrometry; fat tissue may be a less invasive source of material. For assessing renal involvement in AL, quantitative proteinuria/albuminuria matters; serum and urine immunofixation and serum free chains assess the monoclonal protein. Kidney function and immune conditions affect the interpretation of chains. In proven AL amyloidosis, even without cardiac symptoms, cardiac biomarkers and cardiac imaging help establish the presence and severity of cardiac involvement. Applicability: The guideline section concerns amyloid assessment in bone marrow, particularly in plasma cell disorders. It justifies caution about a single specimen but does not give the test's sensitivity specifically after this patient's treatment. The methodological section of ASH 2026 supports checking primary material and typing options. It does not imply an automatic indication for a new biopsy or the choice of a specific organ. An ASH recommendation on suspicion in unexplained proteinuria and assessment of renal involvement. In this patient significant proteinuria is not established; the protein concentration in a single sample does not replace a properly performed quantitative study. A strong ASH 2026 recommendation with low certainty of evidence for proven AL. Here its application depends on clarifying the primary diagnosis or the emergence of a reasonable cardiac suspicion; heart size on CT does not replace this assessment.

“Management of relapsed/refractory AL amyloidosis”. Worsening organ function after a hematological response in AL may reflect irreversible damage or residual production of amyloidogenic chains; a relapse decision requires serial assessment of clone and organs. Applicability: A review of treated, proven AL. Here the primary type, drugs, baseline values and best response are unknown; the complaints alone do not allow applying the relapse category.

“Expert consensus recommendations to improve diagnosis of ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy”. Neuropathy in hereditary ATTR amyloidosis may have varied manifestations and may lack a known family history; with reasonable suspicion, tissue typing and TTR testing are used. Detecting a TTR variant alone does not establish clinically overt hereditary ATTR amyloidosis because of incomplete penetrance; the variant's significance is assessed together with phenotype and tissue data. Applicability: Expert consensus on hereditary ATTR amyloidosis with polyneuropathy. The current complaints are non-specific, and the absence of family cases neither confirms nor excludes ATTR. The same consensus, a separate statement on genetic confirmation. Genetic testing is not proposed as an unconditional test for all patients with paresthesias.

“Diagnostic criteria for small fibre neuropathy in clinical practice and research”. Small fiber neuropathy is assessed by clinical signs combined with quantitative sensory testing and/or intraepidermal fiber density; normal routine nerve conduction is compatible with such involvement. Applicability: A study of diagnostic criteria for small fiber neuropathy. Complaints alone are insufficient; criteria for pure small fiber neuropathy are not transferred mechanically when radiculopathy or focal neuropathy coexists. The test confirms the phenotype, not AL or another etiology.

“Comparison of Magnetic Resonance Imaging with Electrodiagnosis in the Evaluation of Clinical Suspicion of Lumbosacral Radiculopathy”. Clinical picture, MRI and electrodiagnosis assess different aspects of radiculopathy and need to be compared; structural degeneration alone does not prove causation of symptoms. Applicability: A study of lumbosacral radiculopathy. The principle of clinico-anatomical correlation was used, without transferring group accuracy figures to this patient.

“Cancer Pain (PDQ®)–Health Professional Version”. Anticancer therapy can cause a predominantly sensory neuropathy; neurotoxic agents include certain proteasome inhibitors and thalidomide, and manifestations sometimes persist after treatment ends. Applicability: NCI PDQ describes class toxicity. The patient's drugs are unknown, and the symptoms preceded chemotherapy; the source supports checking a possible additional contribution, not attribution to a specific agent.

“Cauda equina, conus medullaris and syndromes mimicking sciatic pain: WFNS spine committee recommendations”. New or progressive neurological deficits in the legs, changes in perineal sensation and urinary dysfunction may require urgent assessment for cauda equina syndrome. With clinical suspicion of cauda equina syndrome, urgent lumbar MRI is recommended, because examination alone is not sensitive enough to exclude compression. Applicability: WFNS 2024 concerns suspected cauda equina compression. Historical frequent urination or chronic inactive radiculopathy do not on their own establish this syndrome. A conditional safety pathway. The current MRI description shows no involvement of the conus or cauda equina; urgent repeat study is tied to a new clinical trigger.

“International Myeloma Working Group Recommendations for the Diagnosis and Management of Solitary Plasmacytomas”. Solitary plasmacytoma requires histological and immunohistochemical confirmation of a clonal plasma cell tumor, absence of additional lesions and myeloma-defining events, and absence of significant clonal bone marrow involvement. When assessing plasmacytoma, it is important to determine clonal bone marrow involvement with a suitable sensitive method and to state the method; an aspirate without proper trephine biopsy/immunohistochemistry or sensitive flow cytometry is insufficient for a full assessment. Applicability: IMWG 2026. Two described lesions do not yet mean two plasma cell tumors, but they do not allow the process to be called solitary until the second lesion is clarified. IMWG 2026. The immunocytology performed is not called a validated MRD study; a negative result does not substitute for the unperformed or undocumented recommended immunohistochemistry.

“Histological and proteomic characterization of musculoskeletal amyloidomas”. Bone amyloid deposits can mimic a tumor; morphology should assess both the amyloid and a possible plasma cell component, and proteomic typing helps when immunohistochemistry is uncertain. Applicability: A series of four musculoskeletal amyloidomas. It justifies a separate morphological check of a rare alternative but does not determine its frequency or probability in this situation.

“Differential diagnosis of hemangiomas from spinal osteolytic metastases using 3.0 T MRI: comparison of T1-weighted imaging, chemical-shift imaging, diffusion-weighted and contrast-enhanced imaging”. Assessment of the fat component, chemical shift, diffusion and contrast enhancement on MRI may help distinguish atypical hemangioma from metastatic vertebral involvement. Applicability: A small primary study; not all lesions had histological confirmation. Numerical accuracy thresholds were not applied; the images themselves need review, not just the text list of alternatives.

“Society of Skeletal Radiology– white paper. Guidelines for the diagnostic management of incidental solitary bone lesions on CT and MRI in adults: bone reporting and data system (Bone-RADS)”. Cortical involvement of the bone lesion and a cancer history are grounds for in-depth radiological/oncological assessment; the single bone lesion scoring algorithms are designed specifically for solitary lesions. Applicability: The patient has two lesions, so a single bone lesion scoring category is not assigned. Only the general meaning of warning features was used, and further checking also relies on sources on plasmacytoma and breast cancer.

“ISUOG Consensus Statement on sonographic assessment of the endometrium: how to perform a gynecological ultrasound scan and report the findings”. Further assessment of incidental endometrial changes is determined by symptoms and the set of ultrasound features; in asymptomatic women, endometrial thickness alone does not make invasive testing automatically necessary. Applicability: ISUOG 2026: a consensus ultrasound algorithm not confirmed by a randomized trial. Here there is a spinal MRI description, with unknown bleeding and menopausal status; ultrasound thresholds were not transferred to MRI.

“Surgical Outcomes of Common Peroneal Nerve Entrapment Neuropathy Associated with L5 Radiculopathy”. Peroneal neuropathy and L5 radiculopathy may coexist; distinguishing them requires the clinical distribution of deficits, neurophysiology and, if needed, nerve imaging. Applicability: A study of selected surgical cases of common peroneal neuropathy. It does not justify surgery for this patient and does not prove the site of compression of the superficial branch.

“The role of high-resolution ultrasound and MRI in the evaluation of peripheral nerves in the lower extremity”. Superficial peroneal nerve involvement produces local sensory manifestations in its territory; ultrasound with clinical and dynamic correlation helps characterize the nerve and possible local causes. Applicability: A review of peripheral nerve anatomy and imaging. Moderate fibrotic changes on ultrasound are not equated with proven compression; a local finding does not explain all four limbs.

“New Definition of Light Chain Monoclonal Gammopathy of Undetermined Significance”. Small free light chain deviations depend on method, age and kidney function; standard intervals may give a false-positive classification of light chain gammopathy. Applicability: A 2025 population study — a screening population. The new intervals were not applied as response criteria for treated AL; specific unread table thresholds were not used. A small pathological clone remains possible in the corresponding clinical context.

“Diagnosis, treatment, and response assessment in solitary plasmacytoma: updated recommendations from a European Expert Panel”. An aspirate may underestimate plasma cell infiltration due to sampling features; trephine biopsy, immunohistochemistry and immunophenotyping are assessed together with clonality. Applicability: European expert recommendation 2018; the statement on material selection was used, without equating the plasma cell percentage alone with a myeloma diagnosis.

“Comprehensive Updates in the Role of Imaging for Multiple Myeloma Management Based on Recent International Guidelines”. With less than 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells, more than one bone lesion is needed to distinguish myeloma from solitary plasmacytoma with minimal marrow involvement. A clonal tumor and proper attribution of bone involvement remain necessary; densitometry does not determine the presence of myeloma. Table 2 lists as laboratory signs of organ damage: calcium more than 1 mg/dL above the upper reference or over 11 mg/dL; creatinine clearance below 40 mL/min or serum creatinine over 2 mg/dL; hemoglobin more than 20 g/L below the lower reference or below 100 g/L. A causal link to the plasma cell process is required. On this page the initial workup includes a blood count, calcium, creatinine, electrophoresis and urine protein assessment; the table also defines the criterion of an involved/uninvolved free light chain ratio of at least 100 with an involved chain concentration of at least 100 mg/L. Applicability: The 2021 review reproduces the IMWG criteria in Table 2 and is not a primary guideline. The exact caveat was checked visually; other printed thresholds were not silently corrected. Two non-specific findings without a proven clone do not establish myeloma. The 2021 review reproduces the IMWG criteria; it is not a new primary guideline. Physical page 5, Table 2 and the initial workup paragraph were rechecked. Thresholds are kept in printed units and with strict inequality signs; comparison requires consistent units, references, date and proper attribution. A missing calcium result is not considered normal, and a single laboratory abnormality does not establish myeloma.

“A Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy: Introduction, Rationale, and Scope”. Cervical myelopathy is a clinical syndrome with impaired fine motor skills/coordination, gait and signs of long tract involvement combined with imaging of cervical cord compression. Applicability: Guideline on degenerative cervical myelopathy. A description of stenosis without corresponding clinical signs does not confirm myelopathy; its scales were not transferred to the thoracic spine.

“A Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Patients With Degenerative Cervical Myelopathy: Recommendations for Patients With Mild, Moderate, and Severe Disease and Nonmyelopathic Patients With Evidence of Cord Compression”. With confirmed cervical compression and radiculopathy, even without clinical myelopathy, an assessment of the risk of its development and clinical follow-up are needed. Applicability: A 2017 weak recommendation with low certainty of evidence. The patient has no full current examination or primary cervical images; the source does not create an indication for surgery.

narrative.text: “Associated conditions in small fiber neuropathy – a large cohort study and review of the literature”. In a study of patients with confirmed small fiber neuropathy, the search for concurrent causes included glycemia, “Separate pathology of the endometrium or uterine junctional zone” and thyroid function by TSH/thyroxine. Applicability: The cohort methods table, not a universal mandatory panel. The thyroid function row specifically was checked visually. The available total T3 is not the assessment described in the table; the individual test set is determined by phenotype and history.

“Pan-Asian adapted ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for the diagnosis, staging and treatment of patients with metastatic breast cancer”. At the initial diagnosis of metastatic breast cancer, biopsy allows confirming histology and testing estrogen, progesterone and HER2 receptors; additional molecular tests should match a specific clinical decision. To assess the extent of metastatic breast cancer, CT with bone imaging or an appropriate FDG PET/CT alternative is used; if spinal cord compression is suspected, MRI is the method of choice, and fracture risk is assessed by structural imaging. Applicability: The 2023 ESMO Pan-Asian adaptation for metastatic cancer. Here metastases are only suspected; the statement supports morphological discrimination before such classification, without treatment prescriptions. The 2023 ESMO Pan-Asian adaptation; the modality is chosen according to the clinical question and studies already done. This is not a recommendation for all available scans or routine brain MRI without indications.

After ranking, the uncertainty could already be formulated as specific clinical questions. The first remaining question was where the primary confirmation and typing of amyloid and the treatment documents are; it mattered because without them it is impossible to distinguish historically proven AL, another type or an unconfirmed diagnosis, or to assess relapse and toxicity. The second remaining question was what the tissue nature of both bone lesions is and what the completed result of the clone assessment is; it mattered because different causes may coexist; neither low plasmacytosis nor the two lytic findings alone classify the process. The third remaining question was what the current neurological phenotype is and whether there are signs of central involvement; it mattered because old complaints and summary ENMG sheets do not replace a current examination, small fiber testing and localization. The fourth remaining question was what the primary histology/stage of the breast cancer and prior bone images are; it mattered because these data are needed to interpret the bone findings and plan a representative check without premature metastatic classification. The fifth remaining question was what the current calcium, kidney function, hemoglobin, methods and exact dates of laboratory results are; it mattered because unmeasured calcium is not normal; undated tests do not create a trend. A separate current laboratory check should reconcile hemoglobin, calcium, renal values and their suitability for classification assessment; a bone marrow clone study does not replace this. The sixth remaining question was whether there are gynecological symptoms and a result of targeted endometrial study; it mattered because bleeding status, menopause and appropriate imaging determine further assessment of the incidental finding. The next remaining question was whether the immunoglobulin free light chain results are comparable by method and whether the values before treatment and at best response are known; it mattered because without this the light chain deviation cannot be classified as a relapse, nor can research reference intervals be applied reliably. In this form the gap ceased to be an abstract lack of information and became a testable condition for changing the diagnostic conclusion.

If there are no current suitable results, completing the assessment requires a blood count with hemoglobin, total calcium and creatinine with a proper kidney function assessment. Separately, serum/urine electrophoresis and immunofixation and serum free light chains are compared; the specimen type and method must match the clinical question. Repeating suitable tests already available is not automatic. This step is not replaced by a bone marrow study and does not depend on prior confirmation of AL; the result was to determine the relationship between these versions: possible AL amyloidosis, bone plasmacytoma? and myeloma without an evident paraprotein? After the last independent review, its exact wording recommendation was applied. The corrected text and the unchanged remainder of the protocol were checked separately; the critic's previous receipt is kept. No new full clinical pass was run for this correction.

In summary, the available data were sufficient for a responsible working candidate, but not for a final diagnosis. The available data allow placing the small fiber neuropathy check first as a working explanation of the widespread sensory-autonomic syndrome, while simultaneously checking the previously reported diagnosis of AL amyloidosis. This does not establish the etiology. Local neurological changes and the bone lesions have their own parallel checks; no bone alternative received an unjustified probabilistic advantage. Therefore, at this stage the protocol did not allow establishing active AL, its relapse or remission without primary verification and course over time; final classification of the bone lesions as myeloma, solitary plasmacytoma or metastases without adequate evidence; prescribing or changing anticancer, immunosuppressive or other treatment on the basis of this candidate; or attributing neurotoxicity to an unidentified drug or automatically establishing myelopathy from stenosis; these decisions remained dependent on new data and the clinician's assessment.

The residual uncertainty was recorded explicitly. The tissue type of the historical amyloidosis, the treatment drugs and baseline response values are not confirmed by primary documents. Some tests have no collection date or unit; these gaps were not filled by assumption. Full neurophysiological protocols are missing. MRI/CT were assessed from clinical descriptions; the patient's images and bone lesion tissue were not reviewed. The literature justifies discriminating rules and checks, not the presence of disease in the patient. Consensus statements, research cohorts and small series have different strength. Rank means check priority, not a percentage probability; several processes may coexist. Independent clinical review and the clinician's decision are needed. This record marked the point where the evidential force of the available data ended and the zone of decisions after new material began.

Further progress depended on results capable of changing the classification: a current neurological examination and small fiber testing; primary biopsies/amyloid typing, treatment regimen and baseline course; expert comparison of both bone lesions, clonality and morphology if indicated; primary breast cancer histology and completion of unavailable clinical results; and current hemoglobin, calcium and renal values with verified dates, units and clinical attribution, together with comparable protein studies. Only after them can the order of hypotheses be revised, the final disease determined and a treatment decision made; until then the protocol remains a reasoned candidate reconstruction prepared for clinician review.

source_library.proposition: Solitary plasmacytoma requires histological and immunohistochemical confirmation of a clonal plasma cell tumor, absence of additional lesions and myeloma-defining events, and absence of significant clonal bone marrow involvement. When assessing plasmacytoma, it is important to determine clonal bone marrow involvement with a suitable sensitive method and to state the method; an aspirate without proper trephine biopsy/immunohistochemistry or sensitive flow cytometry is insufficient for a full assessment.

source_library.applicability: The 2021 review reproduces the IMWG criteria in Table 2 and is not a primary guideline. The exact caveat was checked visually; other printed thresholds were not silently corrected. Two non-specific findings without a proven clone do not establish myeloma. The 2021 review reproduces the IMWG criteria; it is not a new primary guideline. Physical page 5, Table 2 and the initial workup paragraph were rechecked. Thresholds are kept in printed units and with strict inequality signs; comparison requires consistent units, references, date and proper attribution. A missing calcium result is not considered normal, and a single laboratory abnormality does not establish myeloma.
source_library.proposition: With less than 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells, more than one bone lesion is needed to distinguish myeloma from solitary plasmacytoma with minimal marrow involvement. A clonal tumor and proper attribution of bone involvement remain necessary; densitometry does not determine the presence of myeloma. Table 2 lists as laboratory signs of organ damage: calcium more than 1 mg/dL above the upper reference or over 11 mg/dL; creatinine clearance below 40 mL/min or serum creatinine over 2 mg/dL; hemoglobin more than 20 g/L below the lower reference or below 100 g/L. A causal link to the plasma cell process is required. On this page the initial workup includes a blood count, calcium, creatinine, electrophoresis and urine protein assessment; the table also defines the criterion of an involved/uninvolved free light chain ratio of at least 100 with an involved chain concentration of at least 100 mg/L.
source_library.title: Comprehensive Updates in the Role of Imaging for Multiple Myeloma Management Based on Recent International Guidelines

Qualitative, physicochemical and microscopic urine results are kept as known values, not missing data. They do not on their own justify infection or another new diagnosis; numerical thresholds were not invented.

The remaining values of the two blood counts — cell indices and differential — are kept with references; relative and absolute values are not mixed. Minor deviations are not used as standalone evidence of a clone, and undated results do not form a trend.
CT describes degenerative changes and status after cervical fixation; this is the structural context of the local neurological assessment.
The recommendation of additional needle EMG and ultrasound is a source plan; actual subsequent results are recorded separately.
The light chain retelling has a documented discrepancy of the lambda unit with the primary forms; the quantitative estimate from this retelling was not used.
The stated diuresis volume of 1.5 L is kept. Without explicit duration and formal collection it does not become standalone proof of daily protein excretion.

problem_representation.text: A 66-year-old woman with prolonged widespread sensory and autonomic complaints, without a described generalized large fiber polyneuropathy on the 2023/2026 studies. There are chronic L5–S1 radiculopathies and a focal right superficial peroneal neuropathy. Amyloidosis and four courses of unknown chemotherapy were reported historically, but there is no primary typing. Current immunofixation and bone marrow studies do not confirm an overt clone/amyloid; a small deviation of immunoglobulin free light chains does not determine activity. After breast cancer treatment, two indeterminate bone lesions are described — L4 and the left iliac bone. A separate endometrial MRI finding needs gynecological clarification.

workup.label: Current laboratory assessment of the plasma cell process and defining criteria
workup.rationale: First, the available primary forms, collection dates, methods, units and references are reconciled. If there are no current suitable results, completing the assessment requires a blood count with hemoglobin, total calcium and creatinine with a proper kidney function assessment. Separately, serum/urine electrophoresis and immunofixation and serum free light chains are compared; the specimen type and method must match the clinical question. Repeating suitable tests already available is not automatic. This step is not replaced by a bone marrow study and does not depend on prior confirmation of AL.

H1.rationale: Paresthesias, dysesthesias, intolerance of hot water and autonomic complaints without a described generalized large fiber polyneuropathy support this working phenotype. Clinical signs and specific tests are insufficient for confirmation; amyloid and non-amyloid causes remain open.

H10.rationale: An amyloid origin is named in the radiological differential of L4 and the iliac bone but has not been tissue-checked. Even detecting amyloid in the lesion would require typing and a search for a possible local clone, not automatic classification as active systemic AL.

H11.rationale: MRI names atypical hemangioma among the alternatives. A smooth contour and absence of perifocal edema allow a benign explanation, but low T1 signal, enhancement and the cortical defect require assessment of the images themselves. The nature of the iliac lesion remains a separate question.

H2.rationale: The consultation reports amyloidosis in 2024 and four chemotherapy courses, but primary histology and typing are missing. The sensory-autonomic syndrome is compatible but non-specific. Current negative immunofixation and bone marrow studies do not confirm an active clone; relapse or remission cannot be established from these materials.

H3.rationale: A specific alternative amyloid type with sensory and autonomic manifestations. There is no primary typing; the family history contains no confirmed cases, and the cardiac phenotype and TTR variant are not established. The available data are insufficient for a separate ATTR priority.

H6.rationale: The described cervical/thoracic stenoses and widespread sensory complaints require checking a central localization. There are no current data on gait, coordination or long tract deficits. Lumbar MRI does not confirm conus or cauda equina involvement but does not assess the entire cervical and thoracic spine.

H7.rationale: The lytic L4 lesion with a cortical defect is compatible with a plasma cell tumor, but there is no histology. The separate iliac lesion must be characterized before classification as solitary plasmacytoma. Low bone marrow plasmacytosis does not determine L4 histology.

H8.rationale: Two bone lesions justify keeping the alternative, but a plasma cell clone and a myeloma nature of these changes are not proven. Plasma cells are 0.8% in the aspirate and approximately 3% in the trephine specimen; no atypical population was found; there is no overt anemia or elevated creatinine in the given tests. Calcium is unknown.

H9.rationale: The reported invasive breast cancer and two indeterminate bone lesions require morphological and oncological comparison. Native CT describes no other convincing secondary changes, and MRI considers a secondary origin less likely; this is not a final exclusion. Bone histology is missing.

questions.answer: Tissue confirmation and typing have their own role; a single negative bone marrow specimen or paraproteins alone do not establish the full picture. Negativity after unknown treatment does not reconstruct the baseline diagnosis.
applicability_limits: Unverified numerical estimates of post-treatment sensitivity were not used.
questions.question: AL amyloidosis: confirmation of tissue amyloid and typing, the diagnostic meaning of a negative bone marrow biopsy and negative immunofixation after treatment.
questions.rationale: The question concerns different diagnostic levels: detecting a deposit, its type and the state after treatment. A negative result in one specimen does not answer all three.

questions.answer: Relapse and residual damage are distinguished by comparable clone and organ trends. Organ deterioration may persist after a response; complaints alone are not a hematological criterion.
applicability_limits: The review concerns proven AL. The full tabulated response criteria were not applied without baseline data.
questions.question: AL amyloidosis after treatment: distinguishing hematological relapse from residual or progressive neuropathy; organ involvement criteria and the assessment of low free light chain concentrations.
questions.rationale: For relapse, the course of the clone and organs matters, whereas persisting neuropathy may behave differently over time; the source directly distinguishes these situations.

questions.answer: Hereditary ATTR amyloidosis may have no family cases; typing and TTR when indicated help discriminate. A genetic variant alone does not establish clinical disease.
applicability_limits: The consensus does not turn non-specific paresthesias into a specific suspicion for every patient.
questions.question: ATTRv amyloid neuropathy: sensory and autonomic manifestations, absent family history, indications for tissue typing and TTR testing; distinguishing ATTR from AL when free light chains are abnormal.
questions.rationale: The absence of family cases and the finding of a genetic variant have different diagnostic meaning; this is exactly what the ATTR consensus statements clarify.

questions.answer: Routine nerve conduction may be normal in small fiber neuropathy; a combination of clinical signs and proper structural/functional tests is needed.
applicability_limits: Concurrent local lesions call for caution with criteria for pure small fiber neuropathy.
questions.question: Small fiber neuropathy with normal routine ENMG: diagnostic criteria, skin biopsy, quantitative sensory and autonomic testing.
questions.rationale: Clinical signs, structural fiber density and functional tests assess the small fiber phenotype; routine nerve conduction does not substitute for these data.

questions.answer: A targeted workup may include B12, glycemic status and TSH/thyroxine; other tests are chosen by history and phenotype. The research cohort table is not an unconditional panel.
applicability_limits: The detected concurrent abnormality does not prove causation of the neuropathy.
questions.question: Search for correctable causes of small fiber neuropathy: B12 deficiency, impaired glucose metabolism, thyroid function and immune causes; indications for targeted tests.
questions.rationale: The research cohort table confirms which concurrent causes were checked but does not establish a need for the same test set or causation of each abnormality.

questions.answer: MRI, electrodiagnosis and examination complement each other: anatomical degeneration does not equal a causal radicular deficit, and the result is assessed by localization.
applicability_limits: Group-level study accuracy is not transferred to the individual case.
questions.question: Chronic radiculopathy: comparison of needle EMG without active denervation, MRI stenosis and clinical localization; distinguishing radicular involvement from small fiber neuropathy.
questions.rationale: The difference between anatomy on MRI and root function on electrodiagnosis explains the need for their clinical comparison.

questions.answer: Neurotoxic agents can cause or worsen sensory manifestations, sometimes for a long time; individual attribution requires real exposure and temporal correspondence.
applicability_limits: Information about a toxicity class does not identify the patient's unknown drugs.
questions.question: Neuropathy during AL amyloidosis treatment: assessing neurotoxicity of anticancer drugs, the temporal relationship and the difference from amyloid neuropathy.
questions.rationale: Class neurotoxicity makes the exposure a subject for checking; the class name does not establish the drug received by this patient or a causal link.

questions.answer: Cervical myelopathy requires clinical signs and corresponding compression; stenosis alone is insufficient. A separate urgent assessment pathway concerns suspected cauda equina or tumor compression.
applicability_limits: Cervical scales were not applied to the thoracic spine. Urgency depends on new symptoms and localization.
questions.question: Degenerative cervical and thoracic myelopathy: clinical signs, discrimination from peripheral neuropathy and triggers for urgent assessment of spinal cord or cauda equina compression.
questions.rationale: The clinical definition of cervical myelopathy is separated from compression on imaging alone. Separate recommendations on cauda equina and tumor compression define the corresponding safety pathways.

questions.answer: Solitary plasmacytoma requires clonal histology, exclusion of additional lesions, proper bone marrow assessment and absence of myeloma-defining events.
applicability_limits: Low overall plasmacytosis is not proof of the absence of a clone in a focal lesion.
questions.question: Bone plasmacytoma: requirements for biopsy, clonality, bone marrow study and whole-body imaging; the significance of a second bone lesion with low plasmacytosis and no paraprotein.
questions.rationale: For solitary plasmacytoma, tissue clonality and the absence of other lesions are different mandatory parts of the classification; a negative bone marrow does not establish it by itself.

questions.answer: With less than 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells, the caveat about more than one bone lesion distinguishes myeloma from solitary plasmacytoma with minimal marrow involvement. It is applied together with clonal evidence and attribution of the lesions.
applicability_limits: The exact table is a reproduction of criteria in a review; its actual source type is preserved. Two non-specific lesions do not establish myeloma.
questions.question: Criteria for plasma cell myeloma with less than 10% bone marrow plasma cells, several lytic lesions and no M-protein; distinction from solitary plasmacytoma and oligosecretory disease.
questions.rationale: The caveat about the number of bone lesions concerns an already properly assessed clonal plasma cell process, not any two non-specific findings.

questions.answer: If metastatic cancer is suspected, coordinated staging and morphological confirmation with assessment of tumor biology are needed. The scoring system for single bone lesions does not transfer to multiple lesions.
applicability_limits: The 2023 ESMO adaptation sets possible modalities, not a requirement to perform all of them.
questions.question: Breast cancer and indeterminate lytic bone lesions: choice of imaging, the role of biopsy and the limitations of native CT and bone scintigraphy in distinguishing metastases, plasmacytoma and benign lesions.
questions.rationale: The guideline on metastatic cancer directly supports staging and biopsy; the single-lesion algorithm has a different scope and does not replace it.
remaining_questions: The accuracy of the specific scintigraphic protocol for a purely lytic lesion is not determined by these fragments; a negative result of such a study is not used here.

questions.answer: Bone amyloid can mimic a tumor; morphology, typing and a search for a possible local plasma cell component are needed.
applicability_limits: A small series gives no individual probability and does not determine systemic involvement.
questions.question: Bone amyloidoma: radiological similarity to plasmacytoma and metastases, morphological confirmation, amyloid typing and distinguishing a localized from a systemic process.
questions.rationale: Small morphological series show the possibility of tumor mimicry and an occult local clone, which justifies tissue examination but not an estimate of individual probability.

questions.answer: Fat, diffusion and contrast features may help distinguish hemangioma from metastases; in case of uncertainty, the decision needs expert comparison and sometimes tissue.
applicability_limits: Universal numerical thresholds of a small study or the solitary-lesion algorithm were not applied to two sites.
questions.question: Atypical vertebral hemangioma: differences from metastases and plasmacytoma on CT and MRI, significance of a cortical defect and indications for further assessment of an indeterminate lesion.
questions.rationale: The imaging study identifies useful features for comparison, but its small size and incomplete histological verification do not allow adopting a universal threshold.

questions.answer: Bleeding, menopause and the combination of targeted ultrasound features determine further investigation; an incidental mention on MRI is not an automatic indication for biopsy.
applicability_limits: The consensus concerns ultrasound assessment; its thresholds do not transfer to spinal MRI.
questions.question: Incidentally detected endometrial change on non-specialized MRI in an older woman: the role of menopausal status, bleeding, transvaginal ultrasound and indications for biopsy.
questions.rationale: The ISUOG statement concerns specialized ultrasound in connection with symptoms; an incidental endometrial description on spinal MRI does not yet contain these data.

questions.answer: Symptom distribution, neurophysiology and local imaging help separate the peroneal contribution from L5; both processes may coexist.
applicability_limits: Surgical series data are not a recommendation for surgery.
questions.question: Superficial peroneal neuropathy: electrophysiological and ultrasound discrimination from L5 radiculopathy, localization and assessment of potential compression.
questions.rationale: The focal peroneal territory and radicular manifestations may overlap, so clinical correlation is needed even if one of the two diagnostic conclusions is present.

questions.answer: Immunoglobulin free light chain results are interpreted in methodological, age and renal context; aspirate and trephine specimen have different representativeness. A small deviation or a single negative specimen does not establish a final conclusion.
applicability_limits: Screening reference intervals were not turned into response criteria for treated AL.
questions.question: Moderate deviation of the free light chain ratio: the effect of age, kidney function and method, the difference from proof of monoclonality; interpreting a negative bone marrow study after treatment and with a hypocellular aspirate.
questions.rationale: Methodological differences in light chains and the differing representativeness of aspirate/trephine explain caution about any single positive or negative result.

patient_information.answer: There are reports of amyloidosis in 2024 and follow-up biopsies in 2025. Their primary reports and typing are missing; in the current trephine specimen, Congo red staining found no amyloid.
applicability_limits: A retelling, a recommendation and a performed study have different evidential status.
patient_information.question: Which study in 2024 confirmed amyloid and its AL type; are blocks, slides, full biopsy reports from 2024–2025 and typing results available?
patient_information.rationale: There is a retelling of prior biopsies and the diagnosis, but not their primary report; the current negative trephine specimen concerns a different time and material.
